screens.title: Build a Simple Inventory App with Python
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll assemble the pieces you've already learned into a working command-line inventory application. We'll use a single connection function, parameterized queries, and small, focused functions for each Create, Read, Update, and Delete operation. That structure keeps code readable, reduces repeated boilerplate, and makes error handling consistent. You'll see how to create the products table, add and view items with formatted output, update quantities and prices safely, and remove entries while checking whether the delete actually affected any rows. Along the way we'll discuss practical best practices: using a centralized connection function that sets a row factory so rows are accessible by column name, always using parameterized queries to avoid injection, committing after DML operations, and closing connections in finally blocks so resources are released. To ground this, we will walk through the example inventory_app dot P Y file code that implements the menu-driven flow, and then add a small search feature that uses a LIKE query for partial matches. By the end you will understand how small, modular functions form a reliable CLI application and why each defensive step matters in a real program.

screens.title: How we'll validate success
screens.narratorSegment: To know you've built the application correctly, use quick checks that validate both behavior and defensive programming. First, after running the startup sequence your create table function should print a message indicating the products table exists. That confirms schema setup. Second, adding a product and then viewing products should show the new entry with a formatted ID, name, quantity, and price. If you see a duplicate name error, the unique constraint is working. Third, when updating a product provide a non-numeric value for quantity to confirm the application rejects incorrect input and does not modify the row. Fourth, deleting a non-existent ID should inform you that no rows were removed. For each check, look for proper commit behavior and that the database file persists between runs. These small experiments validate both functionality and the best practices: parameterized queries, input validation, commit/rollback, and connection cleanup.

screens.title: Centralized Connection Management
screens.narratorSegment: Centralizing connection setup in a single function is both a convenience and a safety measure. The example uses a get_db_connection function that opens a connection to a single database name and assigns a row factory so query results can be accessed by column name. This reduces duplicated setup code across functions and ensures consistent configuration. For instance, when view_products or add_product need a connection, they call this factory and receive a connection object pre-configured to return rows like dictionaries. The concrete benefit is cleaner code: instead of repeating the connect call and row factory in every function, you have one place to modify if you need to change database settings, enable pragmas, or add logging. A common misconception is that opening and closing connections frequently is always expensive; for small CLI apps using a short-lived connection per operation, this pattern is acceptable and safer than keeping a global open connection that may be forgotten. Always close connections in a finally block to release resources. As a takeaway, treat the connection factory as the canonical place for connection policy and error messaging.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Connection Factory
Definition & rationale

A connection factory returns a configured connection object. It centralizes setup and error handling so all CRUD functions receive consistent behavior.

  • Consistent row access via row_factory enables product['name'] style access.
  • Single point to add logging, timeouts, or PRAGMA statements for SQLite.
  • Safer error messaging and standardized null return if the connection fails.
Example
import sqlite3

DATABASE_NAME = 'inventory_app.db'

def get_db_connection():
  """Establishes and returns a database connection."""
  conn = None
  try:
    conn = sqlite3.connect(DATABASE_NAME)
    conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
    return conn
  except sqlite3.Error as e:
    print(f"Error connecting to database: {e}")
    return None
Concrete uses and pitfalls

Call this function at the start of each operation and close the connection in a finally block. For CLI apps, a short-lived connection per function is simpler and avoids stale global state.

Misconception
Opening connections per operation is always bad. In CLI apps this is acceptable; what matters is proper closure and brief lifetime to avoid locks.
Pro tip
If you move to a long-running service, consider connection pooling instead of repeatedly opening raw connections.
Check your understanding
How would you modify the factory to enable foreign keys or other pragmas for SQLite? Consider where to add that code.
Key Takeaway

One factory function keeps connection policy consistent and simplifies changes across the application.

screens.title: Creating the products table
screens.narratorSegment: The create_table function is a small but essential step: it guarantees the products table exists before any operation runs. The example opens a connection using the factory, executes a CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS statement, commits the change, and closes the connection. This protects the app from runtime failures that occur when a table is missing. A concrete example is useful: when you run the application for the first time, create_table will create a file-based SQLite database and add the products table with columns id, name, quantity, and price. A common error is forgetting to commit the DDL transaction; depending on the database, schema changes may not persist until you commit. Another pitfall is not handling exceptions. Use try-except-finally to print meaningful error messages and always close the connection in finally. As a practical check, run the program, look for the 'Database and products table ready' message, then add a product to confirm subsequent operations succeed. Creating the products table means run a safe create table if not exists on startup, commit the ddl, and close the connection in a finally block to avoid silent failures.. In practical terms, ensure schema exists on startup with create_table. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Create Table
Process: create_table

Open a connection, execute a create table statement with IF NOT EXISTS, commit, and close. Handle errors and report status to the user.

1
Call get_db_connection to obtain a connection object.
2
Execute CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS with the products schema.
3
Commit the transaction and close the connection in finally.
Example DDL
cursor.execute('''
  CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS products (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    quantity INTEGER NOT NULL,
    price REAL NOT NULL
  )
''')
conn.commit()
Key Takeaway

Create tables at startup with IF NOT EXISTS, commit, and always close the connection to prevent locked files or missing schema errors.

Misconception
DDL may seem auto-committed; explicitly calling commit ensures behavior across environments and avoids surprises.
Pro tip
Print a clear startup message so users know the database and table are ready before they interact with the menu.
Check
Run the app, look for the readiness message, then list products to confirm the table exists and is queryable.

Validation rejects empty names and non-numeric quantity or price inputs. This prevents obvious errors. The function then calls the connection factory, prepares an INSERT statement using placeholders, and executes it with a tuple of values. Using parameterized queries — not string concatenation — is vital to avoid injection and to let the database handle escaping. If the name violates the UNIQUE constraint, the code catches an integrity error, prints a helpful message, rolls back the transaction, and closes the connection. A common misconception is to rely on try-except blocks but forget to rollback after a failed DML operation. The pattern here is explicit: on success commit, on integrity or other errors rollback, and always close the connection in finally. Think of this pattern as a contract that preserves data integrity and gives the user clear feedback. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Add Product
Code walkthrough: add_product

Prompt for name, quantity, and price. Validate inputs. Use a parameterized INSERT and handle IntegrityError and other database errors with rollback and final close.

def add_product():
  name = input("Enter product name: ").strip()
  if not name:
    print("Product name cannot be empty.")
    return

  try:
    quantity = int(input("Enter quantity: "))
    price = float(input("Enter price: "))
  except ValueError:
    print("Invalid quantity or price. Please enter numbers.")
    return

  conn = get_db_connection()
  if conn:
    try:
      cursor = conn.cursor()
      cursor.execute("INSERT INTO products (name, quantity, price) VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
                     (name, quantity, price))
      conn.commit()
      print(f"Product '{name}' added successfully.")
    except sqlite3.IntegrityError:
      print(f"Error: Product with name '{name}' already exists.")
      conn.rollback()
    except sqlite3.Error as e:
      print(f"Error adding product: {e}")
      conn.rollback()
    finally:
      conn.close()
Misconception
Catching all exceptions without rolling back can leave the transaction open or in a half-applied state; always call rollback on failures.
Example scenario
A user tries to add an existing product name. The function should catch IntegrityError, tell the user the name exists, rollback, and keep the database unchanged.
Key Takeaway

Do not trust input. Validate, use parameterized queries, and make success and failure paths explicit with commit and rollback.

Check
Try adding an item with a blank name and with text in the quantity prompt to verify validation messages appear and no row is inserted.
Security highlight
Parameterized queries protect the database from injection and remove the need for manual escaping of user input.

Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › View Products
Code: view_products

Execute a SELECT ordered by name, fetchall, and print a formatted table with headers. If no rows return, print a clear message so the user understands the inventory is empty.

def view_products():
  conn = get_db_connection()
  if conn:
    try:
      cursor = conn.cursor()
      cursor.execute("SELECT id, name, quantity, price FROM products ORDER BY name")
      products = cursor.fetchall()

      if products:
        print("
--- Current Products ---")
        print(f"{'ID':<4} {'Name':<20} {'Quantity':<10} {'Price':<10}")
        print("-" * 48)
        for product in products:
          print(f"{product['id']:<4} {product['name']:<20} {product['quantity']:<10} ${product['price']:.2f}")
        print("-" * 48)
      else:
        print("No products in the inventory.")
    except sqlite3.Error as e:
      print(f"Error viewing products: {e}")
    finally:
      conn.close()
Example
Add two products with different name lengths and run view_products to confirm columns align and prices show two decimal places.
Misconception
Assuming print formatting always fits. Test with longer names and adjust the format strings if necessary to avoid wrapping in narrow terminals.
Key Takeaway

Format results for readability, handle empty sets, and use row names to keep the code clear.

Check
Confirm that prices print with two decimals and that the header aligns with the rows for easy scanning.
Pro tip
Keep format strings centralized if you plan to reuse the same display in other commands or scripts.

screens.title: Updating a product (Update)
screens.narratorSegment: The update_product function demonstrates a slightly more complex interaction: you must select a row, present current values, accept optional new values, validate them, and then build an UPDATE that changes only the fields the user specified. The example first shows all products to help the user pick an ID, then fetches the selected row to confirm it exists. It asks for new quantity and price strings; leaving a field blank preserves the old value. When the user provides a new numeric value, parse and validate it before including it in the UPDATE. Build the update clause dynamically by collecting update_fields and update_values so you avoid overwriting with empty strings. Then execute the constructed UPDATE with parameter placeholders and append the ID to the values tuple for the WHERE clause. This pattern prevents S Q L injection because all values remain parameterized. A common mistake is concatenating values into the query string or forgetting to append the ID parameter, which can lead to syntax errors or wrong rows being changed. The closing takeaway is: validate inputs and keep every substitution parameterized.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Update Product
Step-by-step: update_product
  1. Show current products so the user can pick a valid ID.
  2. Query for the chosen ID and confirm the row exists.
  3. Prompt for new quantity and price; accept blank to keep current values.
  4. Validate numeric inputs, collect update fields and values into arrays.
  5. Construct UPDATE with placeholders and execute, then commit.
Key code idea
Build update_fields = [] and update_values = [] then join the fields with commas and append the id to update_values before executing the parameterized UPDATE.
Misconception
Attempting to update every column unconditionally can overwrite valid values with blanks. Only include fields the user intends to change.
Key Takeaway

When allowing optional updates, construct the SET clause dynamically and pass all values as parameters to keep queries safe and correct.

Example
If a product has quantity 10 and you leave quantity blank but give a new price, only price should change and quantity remains 10.
Check
Try updating with invalid numbers to confirm the function aborts the update and reports the input error.

screens.title: Deleting a product (Delete)
screens.narratorSegment: Deleting a product is straightforward but requires defensive checks to avoid silent failures. The example asks the user for a product ID, validates it is numeric, and executes a DELETE WHERE id =? with a parameterized value. After executing the statement, check cursor. rowcount to determine whether any row was affected. If rowcount is greater than zero, commit and inform the user that the product was deleted. If rowcount is zero, no matching ID existed and you should inform the user instead of silently committing. A common learner mistake is to assume DELETE always affects a row without checking rowcount; that can mislead users into thinking data was removed when it wasn't. Also remember to call rollback and print an error message if the DELETE raises a database error. Finally, always close the connection in finally. This pattern gives users accurate feedback and keeps data integrity intact. Deleting a product (Delete) means use cursor.rowcount after delete to confirm a row was removed; only commit on successful deletion and always close the connection.. In practical terms, delete by id and verify deletion using cursor.rowcount. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Verify deletes
keyIdea.text: Use cursor.rowcount after DELETE to confirm a row was removed; only commit on successful deletion and always close the connection.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Delete Product
Safe delete pattern

Validate the ID, run a parameterized DELETE, check cursor.rowcount, commit if a row was removed, otherwise inform the user that nothing matched.

def delete_product():
  view_products()
  product_id = input("Enter the ID of the product to delete: ").strip()
  if not product_id.isdigit():
    print("Invalid product ID. Please enter a number.")
    return

  conn = get_db_connection()
  if conn:
    try:
      cursor = conn.cursor()
      cursor.execute("DELETE FROM products WHERE id = ?", (product_id,))
      if cursor.rowcount > 0:
        conn.commit()
        print(f"Product ID {product_id} deleted successfully.")
      else:
        print(f"No product found with ID {product_id}.")
    except sqlite3.Error as e:
      print(f"Error deleting product: {e}")
      conn.rollback()
    finally:
      conn.close()
Misconception
Trusting deletion without checking rowcount may give false success messages. Always verify affected rows for accurate feedback.
Key Takeaway

Confirm deletes with cursor.rowcount and provide explicit messages to the user to avoid confusion.

Check
Attempt to delete an ID that doesn't exist and confirm the app reports that nothing was removed.
Pro tip
Show the products before asking for deletion so the user can choose the right ID and reduce accidental deletes.

screens.title: Parameterized Queries and Security
screens.narratorSegment: Parameterized queries are the single most important defense against S Q L injection in a program like this. In the example code, every INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and SELECT uses question-mark placeholders with a tuple of values passed separately. This approach delegates escaping and typing to the database driver, preventing malicious input from changing the structure of the S Q L statement. A concrete example: when inserting a product name, passing the name as a parameter ensures a name containing punctuation or S Q L-like text is treated as data, not code. A frequent misconception is that only web apps need to worry about injection; any application that accepts user input and constructs S Q L can be vulnerable. Also remember parameterization is not a substitute for input validation; validate types and required fields to provide better user feedback. Finally, parameterized queries also help with performance because many database engines can reuse prepared statements, though that is an implementation detail beyond this chapter's scope. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Parameterized Queries
Definition

A parameterized query uses placeholders and a separate list of values so the database treats inputs strictly as data. This prevents input from being parsed as SQL code.

Example
cursor.execute("INSERT INTO products (name, quantity, price) VALUES (?, ?, ?)", (name, quantity, price))
  • Prevents SQL injection by separating code from data.
  • Makes error handling simpler because the statement structure is fixed.
  • Works consistently across INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and SELECT statements.
Key Takeaway

Treat every user input as untrusted. Use parameterized queries for all DML operations to keep data safe.

Misconception
Parameterization removes the need for input validation. It does not—validation still provides clearer error messages and guards application logic.
Check
Try entering quotes or SQL-like text in a product name; parameterized queries ensure the input does not break the statement and is saved literally.

screens.title: Error Handling and Transactions
screens.narratorSegment: Robust error handling keeps the application predictable and the data consistent. The pattern used across functions is try to run the database operations, except to catch specific exceptions like integrity errors or generic sqlite3 errors, and finally to close the connection. For write operations, if an exception occurs after executing a DML statement, call rollback to undo partial changes before closing. This approach prevents inconsistent state and avoids leaving open transactions. Presenting clear error messages helps both users and developers—catching ValueError for input parsing and sqlite3. IntegrityError for unique constraint violations allows for tailored messages. A typical mistake is to catch broad exceptions and not rollback or not re-raise when appropriate; that can hide problems. Finally, logging or printing the caught exception text gives actionable information during development. For the CLI app, printing friendly messages and rolling back on failures is a practical balance between usability and correctness. Error Handling and Transactions means wrap db operations with try-except-finally. on dml failure call rollback, close the connection, and supply a helpful error message.. In practical terms, use try-except-finally, rollbacks, and clear messages. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Error Handling
Pattern for robustness
  • Use try around DB logic.
  • Catch specific exceptions first, such as IntegrityError, then generic DB errors.
  • On failure after DML, call conn.rollback() to undo partial changes.
  • Always close the connection in finally to release resources.
Concrete example
When INSERT fails due to duplicate name, catch IntegrityError, print a helpful message, call rollback, and close the connection so the database remains unchanged.
Misconception
Ignoring exceptions or closing without rollback can leave transactions half-applied. Explicit rollback is important for correctness.
Check
Force an error, for example duplicate insert, and verify the database state remained unchanged after the error and rollback.
Pro tip
Print the actual exception message during development to speed debugging; consider quieter logging in production code.

screens.title: Modular Design & Maintainability
screens.narratorSegment: Modular design is the backbone of maintainable code. The inventory application maps each menu option to a dedicated function: add_product, view_products, update_product, delete_product, and an optional search_product_by_name. This segmentation makes each function easy to test and reason about. If you need to change how products display, only modify view_products. If you need to change connection logic, update get_db_connection once. A practical advantage is that unit tests can target each small function independently, and bug fixes rarely require global changes. A frequent novice mistake is creating a single large function that handles menu, input, and all database logic; that quickly becomes hard to read and fragile. Instead, keep the menu loop minimal: display options, parse a choice, and call the appropriate function. This also makes it easier to add features later, such as search or authentication, without touching existing reliable code paths. The closing question to reflect on is: which function would you test first and why? Implement search_product_by_name

Prompt for a search term, add percent wildcards for partial matches, use a parameterized SELECT with LIKE, and display results in the same formatted table as view_products.

def search_product_by_name():
  search_term = input("Enter product name or part of name to search: ").strip()
  if not search_term:
    print("Search term cannot be empty.")
    return

  conn = get_db_connection()
  if conn:
    try:
      cursor = conn.cursor()
      cursor.execute("SELECT id, name, quantity, price FROM products WHERE name LIKE ? ORDER BY name",
                     (f'%{search_term}%',))
      products = cursor.fetchall()

      if products:
        # Format and print results similar to view_products
        pass
      else:
        print(f"No products found matching '{search_term}'.")
    except sqlite3.Error as e:
      print(f"Error searching products: {e}")
    finally:
      conn.close()

Add a new menu option for search and a case where no results match to confirm the user receives a helpful message.

Parameterize LIKE patterns and handle empty results to provide a safe and useful search feature.

Check

screens.title: Common mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: When building a small database application, a few recurring mistakes cause the most friction. First, not closing connections leads to resource leaks and can lock the database file in SQLite. Always close connections in finally blocks. Second, lack of input validation means invalid data or runtime exceptions will interrupt your program and confuse users. Validate required fields and numeric types before attempting database operations. Third, ignoring specific error types or printing generic messages reduces your ability to debug issues. Catch specific exceptions like IntegrityError to give actionable feedback, and log or print the real exception text during development. Fourth, forgetting to commit after DML prevents changes from persisting. Remember to call commit after successful INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE. Lastly, hardcoding configuration such as database names makes scripts harder to reuse; prefer constants or external configuration if you plan to expand. The solution to all of these is a disciplined pattern: validate input, use parameterized queries, commit or rollback explicitly, and always clean up connections. Common mistakes and how to avoid them means close connections, validate inputs, catch specific exceptions, commit changes, and avoid hardcoded configs to keep the app reliable and maintainable.. In practical terms, resource leaks, missing validation, and silent errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Not closing connections
Leads to locks and resource exhaustion. Use finally blocks to close connections every time.
No input validation
Invalid types or empty fields cause runtime errors. Validate early with clear messages.
Silent errors
Catching broad exceptions without rollback or clear messaging hides bugs. Be explicit and informative.
Forgetting commits
DML requires commit to persist. If changes seem lost, check for missing commit calls.
Hardcoded config
Use constants or external config to make scripts reusable and easier to deploy in new environments.
Best response
Adopt a consistent pattern: validate, parameterize, commit/rollback, and close connections. That prevents most common failures.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll assemble the pieces you've already learned into a working command-line inventory application. We'll use a single connection function, parameterized queries, and small, focused functions for each Create, Read, Update, and Delete operation. That structure keeps code readable, reduces repeated boilerplate, and makes error handling consistent. You'll see how to create the products table, add and view items with formatted output, update quantities and prices safely, and remove entries while checking whether the delete actually affected any rows. Along the way we'll discuss practical best practices: using a centralized connection function that sets a row factory so rows are accessible by column name, always using parameterized queries to avoid injection, committing after DML operations, and closing connections in finally blocks so resources are released. To ground this, we will walk through the example inventory_app dot P Y file code that implements the menu-driven flow, and then add a small search feature that uses a LIKE query for partial matches. By the end you will understand how small, modular functions form a reliable CLI application and why each defensive step matters in a real program.

These objectives guide the construction of the inventory application and connect each technical step to a real skill. First, you'll integrate Python database programming concepts—opening connections, executing parameterized S Q L, and fetching results—into a functional command-line application. For example, you'll combine the connection factory with CRUD functions so the application can add and list products. Second, you'll implement full CRUD operations for a products table. That means writing safe insert, select, update, and delete statements and ensuring commits and rollbacks happen where appropriate. Third, you'll design a simple menu-driven interface. A clear menu leads users to small, focused functions and reduces error-prone input handling. Lastly, you'll apply best practices for connection management, parameterized queries, and error handling across the complete app. These practices prevent resource leaks, protect against injection, and make debugging easier. Each objective maps to a verifiable competency milestone so you can confirm you built and tested the application correctly.

To know you've built the application correctly, use quick checks that validate both behavior and defensive programming. First, after running the startup sequence your create table function should print a message indicating the products table exists. That confirms schema setup. Second, adding a product and then viewing products should show the new entry with a formatted ID, name, quantity, and price. If you see a duplicate name error, the unique constraint is working. Third, when updating a product provide a non-numeric value for quantity to confirm the application rejects incorrect input and does not modify the row. Fourth, deleting a non-existent ID should inform you that no rows were removed. For each check, look for proper commit behavior and that the database file persists between runs. These small experiments validate both functionality and the best practices: parameterized queries, input validation, commit/rollback, and connection cleanup.

Centralizing connection setup in a single function is both a convenience and a safety measure. The example uses a get_db_connection function that opens a connection to a single database name and assigns a row factory so query results can be accessed by column name. This reduces duplicated setup code across functions and ensures consistent configuration. For instance, when view_products or add_product need a connection, they call this factory and receive a connection object pre-configured to return rows like dictionaries. The concrete benefit is cleaner code: instead of repeating the connect call and row factory in every function, you have one place to modify if you need to change database settings, enable pragmas, or add logging. A common misconception is that opening and closing connections frequently is always expensive; for small CLI apps using a short-lived connection per operation, this pattern is acceptable and safer than keeping a global open connection that may be forgotten. Always close connections in a finally block to release resources. As a takeaway, treat the connection factory as the canonical place for connection policy and error messaging.

The create_table function is a small but essential step: it guarantees the products table exists before any operation runs. The example opens a connection using the factory, executes a CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS statement, commits the change, and closes the connection. This protects the app from runtime failures that occur when a table is missing. A concrete example is useful: when you run the application for the first time, create_table will create a file-based SQLite database and add the products table with columns id, name, quantity, and price. A common error is forgetting to commit the DDL transaction; depending on the database, schema changes may not persist until you commit. Another pitfall is not handling exceptions. Use try-except-finally to print meaningful error messages and always close the connection in finally. As a practical check, run the program, look for the 'Database and products table ready' message, then add a product to confirm subsequent operations succeed. Creating the products table means run a safe create table if not exists on startup, commit the ddl, and close the connection in a finally block to avoid silent failures.. In practical terms, ensure schema exists on startup with create_table. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The add_product function ties together input validation, parameterized S Q L, and exception handling. It first prompts the user for a name, quantity, and price. When building a small database application, a few recurring mistakes cause the most friction. First, not closing connections leads to resource leaks and can lock the database file in SQLite. Always close connections in finally blocks. Second, lack of input validation means invalid data or runtime exceptions will interrupt your program and confuse users. Validate required fields and numeric types before attempting database operations. Third, ignoring specific error types or printing generic messages reduces your ability to debug issues. Catch specific exceptions like IntegrityError to give actionable feedback, and log or print the real exception text during development. Fourth, forgetting to commit after DML prevents changes from persisting. Remember to call commit after successful INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE. Lastly, hardcoding configuration such as database names makes scripts harder to reuse; prefer constants or external configuration if you plan to expand. The solution to all of these is a disciplined pattern: validate input, use parameterized queries, commit or rollback explicitly, and always clean up connections. Before you code, remember three compact principles. First, centralize connection setup in a factory function that returns a connection configured with row access by name; it simplifies changes and keeps code consistent. Second, always use parameterized queries for all DML and SELECT operations; this protects against injection and makes statements predictable. Third, wrap database operations in try-except-finally blocks and call commit on success and rollback on failure, always closing connections in finally.
